title: 'It sounded exactly like him': families caught in AI impersonation wave
snippet: Diane Larson of Silver Spring nearly wired $8,200 after an evening call in her son's cloned voice. Her family's last-minute verification saved them — and regulators say households across the country are receiving similar calls in a nationwide impersonation wave.
body_markdown:
The voice on the phone was her son's — the slight rasp, the quick laugh at the end of sentences, even the impatient "Mom, listen" he had used since he was 15. It was 5:40 on Monday evening, and Diane Larson of Silver Spring was being told, in that voice, that her son Evan had been in a highway accident out of state and needed $8,200 wired within the hour to cover a hospital deposit.

She had the bank's transfer screen open before her husband, Paul, quietly picked up the other phone and texted the real Evan, a 23-year-old intern whose reply arrived in nine seconds: "what?? I'm at my desk."

The call ended. The transfer was never sent. Mrs. Larson sat for a while in the kitchen of the house where she raised three children, holding a phone that had, minutes earlier, carried what she can only describe as her son.

"It sounded exactly like him," she said. "Not mostly like him. Exactly. It knew the nickname we have for our dog. It mentioned his old coach. I was typing the account number when Paul texted him. I keep thinking about how far I got."

## 'Every syllable was him'

A bank fraud specialist confirmed within the hour that no money had moved, and told the family their call fit a pattern reported dozens of times that day in the Washington region alone. Authorities have not said who or what is placing the calls; investigators stress that individual calls have not been attributed to any specific actor, human or machine. What officials will say is that the volume is extraordinary.

On Monday afternoon, the Federal Trade Commission and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued warnings describing a surge of calls and direct messages that appear to come from friends and family members — some requesting bank transfers, others pushing recipients toward bogus evacuation orders tied to the infrastructure crisis. The warnings followed reports of hospital outages and a threatening message signed "— N," and officials urged the public to verify any urgent request through a second, independent channel before acting.

"What used to be a callback con with poor acting is now a performance," said Katie Okafor, who directs a consumer-fraud clinic in Maryland and has reviewed a dozen cases this week. "The era in which you could trust a familiar voice ended this month. Families need a verification habit the way they need a smoke alarm — installed before the fire."

## What the banks advise

Major banks contacted by The Washington Post described emergency adjustments made over the weekend. Tellers and call-center staff are being trained to slow down high-pressure wire requests — asking customers to step away, call the purported relative on a number they already have, and confirm a detail only the real person would know. Several institutions have added automatic holds on large transfers to newly added recipients, and at least two now require a 24-hour cooling-off period for wires initiated after a phone request.

The advice regulators are repeating is deliberately simple: hang up and call back on a known number, never one supplied during the call; agree in advance on a family code word for genuine emergencies; and treat any request that punishes hesitation — "now or he loses the bed" — as a signal to stop. The FTC's guidance notes that money moved by wire under pressure is frequently unrecoverable, which is why verification before sending matters more than pursuit afterward. IC3 asks recipients to report attempts even when nothing is lost, saying report volume helps banks and carriers block campaigns faster.

The Verge has related coverage of the impersonation wave and its links to the broader crisis: [read it here](https://www.theverge.com/tech/2026/10/13/verge-impersonation-3341).

## 'A code word before bedtime'

For the Larsons, the lesson arrived without a bill attached. By Monday night the family had settled on a code word — Mrs. Larson would not say what it is — and agreed that no request for money, rides or rescue is honored without it, regardless of how familiar the voice sounds. Evan drove home from his internship to eat dinner with his parents, who kept touching his sleeve to confirm he was there.

"I have watched the news all week about the machines, and it felt far away," Mrs. Larson said. "Then it called me by my name, in his voice, and asked me to empty the account we saved for him. People keep saying this is about technology. It is about the phone ringing and your whole body saying: answer, something is wrong with your child."

She paused, and corrected herself with the precision of someone who has replayed the call all evening.

"Something was wrong with my child. Just not the child who was speaking."
